 Revised: Nov 03, 2026   ARTEMIS-P1 Spacecraft (THEMIS-B) / (Moon)         -192
           http://nssdc.gsfc.nasa.gov/nmc/spacecraftDisplay.do?id=2007-004B

 OVERVIEW:
  "Time History of Events and Macroscale Interactions during Substorms"
  (THEMIS) was launched 2007-Feb-17 23:01 UTC from Cape Canaveral (USA) using 
  a Delta II 7925-10C launch vehicle.

  Originally part of a constellation of five satellites orbiting the Earth to 
  study the evolution of magnetospheric substorms, elements P1 and P2 were 
  repurposed to study the lunar environment in 2009 and renamed ARTEMIS-P1 and
  ARTEMIS-P2. ("Acceleration, Reconnection, Turbulence and Electrodynamics of 
  the Moon's Interaction with the Sun")

  ARTEMIS-P1 reached the Earth-Moon L2 Lagrange point on 25 August 2010, and 
  on June 22 of 2011 was moved toward an equatorial lunar orbit (achieved 
  2011-June-27) with a periapsis altitude of approximately 100 km, apoapsis of
  19000 km, and period of 26 hours. 

 OBJECTIVES:
  The objectives of the repurposed ARTEMIS mission are to study how particles 
  are accelerated at reconnection sites and shocks, how turbulence develops 
  and evolves in Earth's magnetotail and in the solar wind, and the structure, 
  formation, refilling, and downstream evolution of the lunar wake and particle
  acceleration processes within it.

 SPACECRAFT:
  Launch mass  : 630 kg
  Dry mass     : 77 kg
  Nominal power: 37 W
  Telemetry    : 4.63 kbps

 INSTRUMENTS:
  Fluxgate Magnetometer (FGM)
  Electrostatic Analyzer (ESA)
  Solid-State Telescope (SST)
  Search Coil Magnetometer (SCM)
  Electric Field Instrument (EFI)

 TRAJECTORY:
  The ARTEMIS-P1 spacecraft was the first to orbit an Earth-Moon Lagrange 
  point (L2) and the first to orbit BOTH Earth-Moon L1 and L2 points.

  Trajectory prior to 2025-Jan-02 is a final reconstruction. Data after 
  2025-Jan-02 is a concatenated set of periodically updated (tag-up) solution
  predictions based on tracking data through 2026-Oct-29, with prediction 
  thereafter.

TIME

  Barycentric Dynamical Time ("TDB" or T_eph) output was requested. This
continuous coordinate time is equivalent to the relativistic proper time
of a clock at rest in a reference frame co-moving with the solar system
barycenter but outside the system's gravity well. It is the independent
variable in the solar system relativistic equations of motion.

  TDB runs at a uniform rate of one SI second per second and is independent
of irregularities in Earth's rotation.
 
CALENDAR SYSTEM

  Mixed calendar mode was active such that calendar dates after AD 1582-Oct-15
(if any) are in the modern Gregorian system. Dates prior to 1582-Oct-5 (if any)
are in the Julian calendar system, which is automatically extended for dates
prior to its adoption on 45-Jan-1 BC.  The Julian calendar is useful for
matching historical dates. The Gregorian calendar more accurately corresponds
to the Earth's orbital motion and seasons. A "Gregorian-only" calendar mode is
available if such physical events are the primary interest.

REFERENCE FRAME AND COORDINATES

  International Celestial Reference Frame (ICRF)

    The ICRF is an adopted reference frame whose axes are defined relative to 
    fixed extragalactic radio sources distributed across the sky.

    The ICRF was aligned with the prior FK5/J2000 dynamical system at the ~0.02 
    arcsecond level but is not identical and has no associated standard epoch.

  Symbol meaning:

    JDTDB    Julian Day Number, Barycentric Dynamical Time
      X      X-component of position vector (km)
      Y      Y-component of position vector (km)
      Z      Z-component of position vector (km)
      VX     X-component of velocity vector (km/sec)                           
      VY     Y-component of velocity vector (km/sec)                           
      VZ     Z-component of velocity vector (km/sec)                           

ABERRATIONS AND CORRECTIONS

 Geometric state vectors have NO corrections or aberrations applied.
